cls: Anthraquinone derivative - interleukin-1 beta (IL-1) inhibitor (slow-acting symptomatic agent for osteoarthritis)
quick: 50 mg once daily for first 4 weeks, then 50 mg twice daily
Take with food (with meals) to reduce GI upset
Avoid - not recommended; insufficient safety data
Reduce dose if CrCl <30 mL/min; avoid in severe impairment
Contraindicated in liver disease / history of liver disease
summary: Uniflexin is a brand of diacerein, an anthraquinone derivative that inhibits interleukin-1 beta and is used as a slow-acting symptomatic treatment for osteoarthritis (notably hip and knee). It is not FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF/national data. Its onset is delayed (weeks), diarrhoea is very common, and European regulators have restricted its use because of severe diarrhoea and hepatotoxicity - it is contraindicated in liver disease and should be started at a reduced dose.
indications: Symptomatic treatment of osteoarthritis of the hip and knee (second-line, slow-acting)

dosage.n: For the first 4 weeks, taken with the evening meal, to limit diarrhoea
With morning and evening meals after the initial 4 weeks

admin: Take with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Start at 50 mg once daily for 4 weeks before increasing, per regulatory risk-minimisation measures
Stop treatment if diarrhoea occurs and seek medical advice
Effect is slow in onset - may take several weeks; not for acute pain relief
moa: Diacerein and its active metabolite rhein inhibit the synthesis and activity of interleukin-1 beta (IL-1) and reduce IL-1-induced production of metalloproteinases and other catabolic mediators in cartilage. This decreases cartilage degradation and inflammation in osteoarthritic joints, producing a slow-acting symptomatic and possibly structure-modifying effect without direct cyclo-oxygenase inhibition.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to diacerein, anthraquinone derivatives, or excipients
Inflammatory bowel disease / intestinal obstruction or pseudo-obstruction
Children under 65 years are not the issue - use restricted in patients over 65 (see relative)
relative: Patients older than 65 years (start at reduced dose, monitor closely)

preg: Use is not recommended in pregnancy because of insufficient safety data; avoid unless clearly necessary.
lact: Diacerein/rhein metabolites can be excreted in milk (anthraquinones); breastfeeding should be avoided during treatment.
renal: Reduce the dose by half in patients with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, and avoid in severe renal impairment.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with current or past liver disease because of the risk of hepatotoxicity. Discontinue if signs of liver injury (jaundice, raised transaminases) develop.

moderate: Laxatives (additive diarrhoea, risk of dehydration and hypokalaemia)
Other hepatotoxic drugs (additive liver injury risk)
Drugs affected by hypokalaemia, e.g. digoxin (if diarrhoea causes potassium loss)
minor: Aluminium/magnesium antacids (may reduce absorption if taken together)
interactions.food: Food reduces GI side effects; antacids taken simultaneously may lower absorption
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excess - adds to hepatic burden
interactions.diagnostics: Causes harmless yellow-brown discoloration of urine; may elevate liver enzymes

serious: Severe/persistent diarrhoea with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
emergency: Severe dehydration / electrolyte collapse from profuse diarrhoea

monitoring: Liver function tests before and periodically during treatment
Bowel habit - stop drug if significant diarrhoea develops
Hydration and serum potassium if diarrhoea occurs
counsel: Take with meals; expect a delay of several weeks before benefit
Your urine may turn yellow-brown - this is harmless
If you develop loose stools or diarrhoea, stop the medicine and contact your doctor
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or right upper abdominal pain (liver warning)
Drink adequate fluids; do not combine with laxatives
pk: Slow - symptomatic benefit appears after several weeks of regular use
Active metabolite rhein peaks ~2.5-4 hours after dosing (delayed by food)
Carry-over effect persists for weeks after stopping (slow-acting agent)
Store below 25-30 C, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Uniflexin is a brand name for diacerein; not FDA-approved - record based on EMA/SmPC and BNF
EMA restricted use after a 2014 review: start at 50 mg once daily, avoid in liver disease, and avoid in patients over 65 unless carefully assessed
Diarrhoea is the most common adverse effect and a reason to stop treatment
Slow onset of action - not for acute pain; full benefit takes weeks
Causes benign yellow-brown urine discoloration via rhein metabolite
missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as remembered, unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the normal schedule. Do not double the dose. Because the drug is slow-acting, an occasional missed dose has little immediate impact.
overdose: Overdose is expected to cause severe diarrhoea with dehydration and electrolyte loss. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with fluid and electrolyte replacement and monitoring of liver and renal function.
